FULL NARRATION
The Bible begins where Israel began, with Israel's daily confession. Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One. Jesus called it the most important commandment. The first Christians were Jews who prayed these words, and they never stopped. There is one God and no other.

Paul takes Israel's own confession and speaks of one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. The Father is God. The Bible gives no picture of him, and this film doesn't draw one. Jesus taught his followers to pray to our Father in heaven.

John opens his Gospel this way. In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. With God, and God. When Thomas meets the risen Jesus behind locked doors, he calls him my Lord and my God. The Son is fully God, and in Jesus he also became fully man.

The Spirit is not a force God uses. The Bible speaks of him as God. When Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit, Peter told him he had not lied to men, but to God. And the Spirit is everywhere, as only God is. Where can I go to escape Your Spirit? Where can I flee from Your presence?

At the Jordan the three are seen together, and none of them is the other. The Son comes up out of the water. The Spirit descends on him like a dove. And the Father speaks from heaven. You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased. The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Spirit.

The risen Jesus sends his followers out, baptizing in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. One name. Christians say God is one in being and three in persons, each fully God, and one God. Or more simply: one what, three whos. Not three gods. Not one person in three masks. Not three parts.

Every picture from inside the world breaks, and each teaches an old mistake. Water as ice, liquid, and steam is one thing in three forms. That's one person in three masks. A clover makes each person a third of God, when each is wholly God. Three people sharing one nature would be three gods. The church weighed these long ago and set them aside. To whom will you liken God? To what image will you compare Him?

So instead of a picture, Christians keep the Bible's words and the creed's. The Nicene Creed calls the Son God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God. The family catechism calls this not a riddle to solve but a wonder to receive. God has always been love.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.

In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. Genesis opens with God already there. Nothing comes before him, and nothing helps him. Christians confess that God made all things, seen and unseen, out of nothing, by the word of his power.

Day by day the empty world is given shape and then filled. Six times God calls what he made good. The seventh time, very good. The world is not a mistake or a prison. It's a gift.

Being made in God's image means we were made to know him, to reflect his character, and to rule over and care for his world as those who answer to him. We were made for God himself.

Image and work arrive together. God blesses the man and the woman and gives them the earth to rule and to care for on his behalf. To tend it and keep it, not to spoil it for themselves.

The image is given, not earned. A newborn, a man with advanced dementia, and the most gifted adult in the room have the same worth, because their worth was never a ranking of what they can do. Many who don't believe in God hold the same belief, and live it well.

That God created, that he created from nothing, and that humanity bears his image are what all Christians confess. The age of the earth and the way God created are open questions, and faithful Christians who love the same Bible have landed in different places. Jesus summed up what God asks in two commands. Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength. And love your neighbor as yourself. Made for that love, people were joined to God, to each other, to themselves, and to the world he gave them.

In Genesis three, the serpent doesn't start with the fruit. He starts by making God sound mean. Then he makes a promise: you will be like God. At its root, sin is not trusting that God is good, and wanting to be our own god, deciding good and evil for ourselves.

The damage runs in every direction at once. They hide from God. They cover their shame. They blame each other. And the ground grows thorns. Isaiah says it plainly. Your iniquities have built barriers between you and your God.

The family catechism defines it. Sin is any failure to love God and others as we should, whether by doing what God forbids or by failing to do what he commands. It's more than a list of wrong things done. It's love turned in on ourselves.

Paul says it without exception. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. No one is outside it and no one is above it, the people who wrote the Bible included. But the same sentence goes straight on to grace.

Judgment is never the only word. God comes looking and calls: where are you? Jesus said he came to seek and to save the lost. At the cross God himself mends what sin broke. And the way home stays open. If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins.

All Christians confess that every person has sinned and needs God's grace, and that God himself comes to save. How the first sin reaches everyone after it is debated, and churches word it differently. This film doesn't choose between them.

The way home stays open.

The Gospels don't hide his humanity. Weary from walking, he sits down by a well. At his friend's tomb, Jesus wept. Hebrews says he was tempted in every way that we are, yet without sin.

Only someone who is both could bring God and people back together. As man he could stand in our place. As God he could carry what no one else could.

One person, truly God and truly man.

The creed says he was crucified also for us under Pontius Pilate. The chief priests and their council handed him over. Pilate, the Roman governor, condemned him. Roman soldiers crucified him. Jesus himself, his disciples, and the first church were Jews, and blaming the Jewish people for his death is a lie that Christians must reject plainly. The New Testament places all of us inside the guilt.

At the first Passover a lamb died in the place of the firstborn, and Israel went free. Jesus died at Passover, and Paul says it. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.

A ransom was the price paid to set a slave or a prisoner free. For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many. Peter says the price was not silver or gold but Christ himself. He paid it with his own life, freely given.

Isaiah saw a servant who suffered for others. The punishment that brought us peace was upon Him. This is not an angry Father against an unwilling Son. Jesus said he lays his life down of his own accord. The one who bears it is God himself in the Son.

Many early Christian writers loved this picture. By his death Jesus broke the power of the one who holds the power of death, and set free those held in slavery by their fear of death. He disarmed the powers, triumphing over them by the cross.

But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us. The cross does not change God's heart toward us. It shows it. Some Christians put this picture at the center: the love seen at the cross changes those who see it.

Reconciled was the word for making peace between people at war. Here the one who was wronged, God, makes peace and pays the cost himself.

No one picture says it all. Christians hold them together, and some traditions put one at the center. The creed doesn't choose a theory. It says he came for us men and for our salvation. Christians read Isaiah's servant as Jesus, and many Jewish readers read him as the people of Israel. This film doesn't choose between the ways of explaining the cross.

And the cross is not the end of the story. On the third day the tomb was empty.

FULL NARRATION
Christians confess that Jesus died and was buried. Joseph of Arimathea, a disciple, laid the body in his own new tomb cut into the rock, and rolled a great stone across the entrance. The summary Paul passed on puts the burial between the death and the rising, because the one who was raised is the one who was buried.

Very early on the first day of the week, the women came with the spices they had prepared. They found the stone rolled away, and they did not find the body. All four Gospels tell of the empty tomb that morning. The question they were asked is the whole story in one sentence. Why do you look for the living among the dead? He is not here; He has risen!

John tells of Mary Magdalene weeping outside the tomb. She took the risen Jesus for the gardener until he said her name. He sent her to his brothers with a message, and she went and told the disciples. I have seen the Lord! The first news of Easter was a message to be carried.

The risen Jesus is not a ghost or a memory. He told his frightened friends to look at his hands and feet, and he ate broiled fish in front of them. Yet his body was also changed. He came among them behind locked doors, and he was not always recognized at first. Christians confess that God raised the same body that had been buried, now made new.

Jesus had called Lazarus out of his tomb, still bound in strips of linen, back to the life he had before. Jesus' own rising was different. He was raised into a life on the far side of death. Death no longer has dominion over Him.

Under the law, Israel brought the first sheaf of the harvest to the priest: the first sheaf, and the promise of the rest. Paul uses that picture for Easter. But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile. Because he was raised, the forgiveness won at the cross is sealed, death is not the final word over anyone who belongs to him, and the body and the world God made matter. Every Sunday gathering is a small Easter. It doesn't take away grief. It gives grief a hope.

Because I live, you also will live.

The story starts with a gift, not a problem. God made human beings in his own image, to know him and show what he is like, and to love him and be happy in him forever. Nothing stood between people and God.

People turned from God to their own way, and every one of us has followed. Sin is more than a list of wrong things done. It's a break: with God, with each other, inside ourselves.

Every age builds its towers: be good enough, try harder, earn your way back. The Bible says plainly that the gap is too wide. Salvation is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast. That's hard news for anyone who likes to earn things, and good news for anyone who knows they can't.

Then God crosses the gap from his own side. The Father sends the Son, not to win over an unwilling God, but because he already loves the world. For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life. The eternal Son becomes one of us, fully God and fully man.

At the cross the break is mended, and God is the one who mends it. The Father and the Son are not on opposite sides here. For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God.

He was buried, and on the third day he was raised, in his body, not as an idea. The resurrection is God's sign that the cross did what it set out to do.

The gift is received, not earned. Jesus said to repent and believe in the gospel: turn around, and trust him. Faith is not a work that pays for anything. It's empty hands taking what is given.

God gives more than a clean record. Those who belong to Christ are forgiven, adopted as God's children, given the Holy Spirit, and joined to his people. If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.

All Christians confess that sinners are saved by God's grace, through Jesus' death and resurrection, and not by their own good deeds. Churches differ on the place of baptism, on how God's choosing and our choosing fit together, and on whether a believer can fall away. This film doesn't choose between them.

The story ends where it began, with God and his people together, and more than before. Christians differ on many details of the last things. On this hope they speak together.

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM

All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
A wage is owed. A gift is not. The Bible's word for the gift is grace: the free and undeserved favor of God, who gives sinners what they could never earn and forgives what they could never repay. For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Jesus told of a landowner who paid those who had worked one hour the same as those who had worked twelve. The early workers grumbled, and he answered that he had wronged no one. Or are you envious because I am generous? Grace offends anyone who is keeping count.

Grace is not God grading on a curve. He didn't wait for sinners to put things right. He paid the debt himself, while we were still his enemies. The cross is what the gift cost.

So salvation is received, never achieved: by grace, through faith, not by works. Faith is not the one good deed that earns it. Faith is the empty hand that takes what is given.

Does that make sin safe? Paul heard the question and answered it at once. Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? Certainly not! The grace that forgives also teaches. Good works are not the root of salvation. They are its fruit.

And grace doesn't stop at the door. Paul pleaded three times for a weakness to be taken away, and it was not. He was given this instead. My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness. Grace enough for the day, and God's power at its clearest where ours runs out.

The gift is meant to travel. People who know they have been forgiven, forgive. People who know that everything they have was given, give. In the church no one has anything they did not receive.

All Christians confess that salvation is God's gift, received by grace and not earned. They differ on how God's grace and the human will relate, and on how grace is received: by faith alone, or by faith with the sacraments and the life of the church. This film takes no side.

Grace is the gift that no one earns.

0:17 Abraham
0:40 A mustard seed
0:53 An honest prayer
1:10 How faith grows
1:23 Faith and faithfulness
1:43 Walking on

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
Hebrews 11:1: "Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see."
Genesis 15:6: "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness."
Hebrews 12:2: "Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith"
Mark 9:24: "I do believe; help my unbelief!"
Romans 10:17: "Consequently, faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ."
James 2:17: "So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead."
2 Corinthians 5:7: "For we walk by faith, not by sight."
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Faith, in the Bible's sense, is trust in God and in what he has promised. It's not a leap in the dark, and it doesn't grow stronger the less evidence it has. It's the answer a person gives to someone who has spoken and has proved reliable.

Abraham is the pattern. Old and childless, he was told his family would be like the stars, and he believed, centuries before the law. Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness. The same Abraham also doubted and schemed. Biblical faith is not a flawless mood. It's reliance that is tested and deepened.

In the Gospels, faith is not a force the believer generates. It's reliance on Jesus himself, which is why a mustard seed of it is enough. Its strength was never in the believing. It's in the one believed.

A father brought his suffering son to Jesus, and prayed one of the most honest prayers in the Gospels. I do believe; help my unbelief! His faith was mixed and struggling, and Jesus answered it. Doubt brought to Jesus is still coming to Jesus.

Faith grows the way trust between persons grows: by hearing and remembering what the other has said and done. That's why Scripture keeps retelling the exodus, and why Paul ties faith to hearing the word.

The Bible's word for faith is also its word for faithfulness, so trust doesn't stay private. It obeys, endures, and keeps its promises. Churches describe the link between faith and works in different words, and none of them teaches that faith earns salvation. This film takes no side.

Hebrews eleven is a list of people who acted on what God had said without seeing the outcome. Many died still waiting. Faith doesn't deny the darkness. It holds to the one who has spoken in it, and walks on. For we walk by faith, not by sight.

Its strength is in the one believed.

0:15 Joined to Christ
0:30 Adopted
0:44 Fruit
1:07 Gifts
1:21 Where churches differ

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
Romans 8:9: "And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ."
John 15:5: "I am the vine and you are the branches."
Galatians 4:6: "God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts"
Galatians 5:22-23: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control."

All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity, fully God, who dwells in believers and gives them life with God. He is not a force or a feeling. He is God himself, living in his people.

The Spirit unites believers to Christ. Jesus' own picture is a vine and its branches. The branch lives because it is joined to the vine. I am the vine and you are the branches. Apart from him they can do nothing.

To be adopted means God makes people his own children, with a sure place in his family. Paul says God sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, calling out to God as Father. Abba is the Aramaic word for father.

This is the lifelong work of the Spirit, by which believers grow to be more like Jesus. Paul names nine kinds of fruit. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Fruit grows slowly, and it grows because the branch is joined to the vine.

The Spirit gives gifts to each believer, and they are given for the good of all: teaching, serving, encouraging, giving, leading, showing mercy. Paul's picture is the body, where every part is needed.

Christians agree that the Holy Spirit is God, gives new life, lives in every believer, and gives gifts to build up the church. Churches differ on whether some gifts, such as tongues, prophecy, and healing, continue as they did in Acts, and on whether the baptism of the Spirit is a distinct experience after a person first believes. This film doesn't choose between them.

Even prayer is not left to believers alone. When they don't know how to pray, the Spirit himself intercedes for them. The Spirit helps us in our weakness. The Spirit is not a reward for the strong. He is help for the weak.

He is God himself, living in his people.

The church is the whole company of God's people, gathered by the Spirit around Christ, called to worship God, love one another, and make him known to the world. A building is only where some of them meet.

Paul's picture is a body: many parts, different gifts, one life. No part can say it doesn't need the others, and none is a spare.

Peter's picture is a house of living stones. God is building his people into a dwelling for himself, and the stone the whole house rests on is Christ.

God saves us into a family, not alone. Strangers become members of one household, brothers and sisters who help one another follow Jesus all the way home.

They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. That was the first church in Jerusalem. Christians still gather to worship God, hear his Word, share the Lord's Supper, and help one another.

The church is gathered to be sent. Jesus' last command was to make disciples of all nations, and his last promise was his own presence to the end of the age. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.

Churches share the confession of one Lord and the command to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. They differ on who should be baptized and how, and on how churches are led: by bishops, by elders, or by the congregation deciding together. Faithful churches differ on these while confessing one Lord, and this film doesn't choose between them.

The church is a people, gathered to be sent.

1 Corinthians 11:26: "For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes."
Romans 6:4: "we too may walk in newness of life."
Acts 2:39: "This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off"
Ephesians 4:5: "one Lord, one faith, one baptism"
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Jesus' last command to his disciples included baptism: make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. From the church's first day, those who received the message were baptized.

Paul passes on what he received. On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and said it was his body, given for them: do this in remembrance of me. The cup, he said, is the new covenant in his blood. For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.

Both point to the same thing: Jesus' death and resurrection. Paul says believers were buried with Christ through baptism so that they may walk in newness of life. Churches agree that repentance, faith, and baptism belong together in the New Testament, and that the Supper is received with self-examination and love.

Some churches baptize the children of believers, pointing to Peter's promise to you and your children. Others, Baptists and many evangelicals among them, baptize only those who confess faith for themselves, noting that in Acts those who received the message were baptized. Both read the same chapters carefully.

Some churches pour or sprinkle water. Others immerse, taking the person under the water and up again, a picture of burial and rising. Churches also differ on what baptism does. Catholic, Orthodox, and Lutheran Christians hold it to be a sacrament through which God grants forgiveness and the Spirit. Reformed and Presbyterian churches call it a sign and seal of the covenant of grace. Baptists and many evangelicals call it an ordinance, the commanded public sign that follows faith.

Roman Catholic teaching holds that the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood. Lutherans confess Christ's true body and blood present in, with, and under the bread and wine. Reformed churches teach a real spiritual feeding on Christ by faith. Many Baptist and free churches stress a memorial meal of remembrance and proclamation. All agree that the meal proclaims the Lord's death until he comes.

Paul writes of one Lord, one faith, one baptism. Faithful churches differ on these questions while confessing that one Lord, and this film doesn't choose between them. How your own church practices baptism and the Supper, and why, is a good question to bring to a parent or a pastor.

Both point to Jesus' death and resurrection.

the-bible.description:
A short, clear film on what Christians believe, read straight from the Bible. Where faithful Christians differ, the film names the views and takes no side.

Watch, read every word, and study further: https://www.livewellbyjamesbell.co/study/explorer/watch/the-bible

CHAPTERS

0:25 Speakers and writers
0:50 Scroll, ink and language
1:09 Copies
1:27 From scroll to book
1:49 Which books
2:17 Translation

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
Hebrews 1:1: "On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets."
Romans 16:22: "I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord."
2 Timothy 4:13: "my scrolls, especially the parchments."
Colossians 4:16: "After this letter has been read among you, make sure that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans"
2 Timothy 3:16: "All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness"
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
The Bible's books were written over many centuries, in palaces and in exile, in prison cells and on the road. Their writers include kings, priests, prophets, court officials, a tax collector, a physician, fishermen, and a former Pharisee. Many books name no author at all. Christians believe God was at work in the whole of it.

Prophets spoke and helpers wrote. Baruch wrote on a scroll all the words Jeremiah dictated, and when the king burned that scroll, Jeremiah dictated it again. Paul usually dictated his letters to a secretary and added a greeting in his own hand. One of those secretaries signs his own name in Romans. I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.

Books were written on scrolls of papyrus or of prepared animal skin, in ink, with a reed pen. The Old Testament is in Hebrew, with a small part in Aramaic, a related language. The New Testament is in Greek. Paul once asked a friend to bring him his scrolls, especially the parchments.

Copies were made almost at once. Paul asked one church to pass its letter on to another, and to read the one sent there. Every copy was made by hand until printing came, and every hand-made copy differs from every other in small ways. That's why scholars compare the copies.

From very early on, Christians preferred the codex, a book of folded sheets stitched at the spine, to the scroll. It was cheaper, since it used both sides of the sheet. It was easier to carry and to search. And it could hold all four Gospels, or all of Paul's letters, in one volume. Nearly all early Christian copies are books of this kind.

The churches received as Scripture the books that came from the apostles and their circle, taught the faith handed on in all the churches, and were read in worship across the Christian world. Behind those tests was the conviction that the church was recognizing books that had already proved themselves. Christians of different traditions account for this differently, and Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include further books in the Old Testament. This film doesn't choose between them.

Translation is part of the Bible's own story. The New Testament itself puts some of Jesus' Aramaic words into Greek. Jews made the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures that the first churches outside Judea read, and the New Testament was in Latin, Syriac, and Coptic by the third century. Every translation is a set of decisions, which is why it helps to read more than one.

All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness.

A short, clear film on what Christians believe, read straight from the Bible. Where faithful Christians differ, the film names the views and takes no side.

0:00 Prayer
0:17 The pattern Jesus gave
0:40 Praise and thanks
1:08 Confessing
1:22 When the answer is not what we asked
1:47 When there are no words

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
Matthew 6:10: "Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven."
Psalm 100:4: "Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise"
Philippians 4:6: "Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God."
1 John 1:9: "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins"
Luke 22:42: "Yet not My will, but Yours be done."
Romans 8:26: "the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words."
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Prayer is talking with God, who is our Father: bringing him worship, thanks, confession, and requests, and trusting that he hears because of Jesus. It's not a way of getting things out of God. It's a child speaking to a father.

When his disciples asked him to teach them to pray, Jesus gave them a pattern, the Lord's Prayer. God's name honored. His kingdom and his will first. Then daily bread, forgiveness as we forgive, and protection from evil. Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Christians all over the world still pray it.

Praise tells God who he is. Thanks tells him what he has done. The psalms, the Bible's own book of prayers and songs, are full of both.

Paul tells worried people not to swallow their worry but to turn it into prayer, with thanks. Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. Asking is not bothering God. It's what children do with a father who loves them.

Confession is neither groveling nor hiding. When we sin we confess it to God, who is faithful and just to forgive us because of Jesus, and we turn from it. There is no sin too big for the cross.

Prayer is not a promise that we will get what we ask. Jesus himself asked his Father in the garden to take the cup of suffering away, and added these words. Yet not My will, but Yours be done. Some prayers, even for someone to get better, are not answered the way we longed for, and that hurts. The Bible doesn't hide it. Many of its prayers ask God: how long, O LORD?

Paul says that when we don't know how we ought to pray, the Spirit himself prays for us, with groans too deep for words. Prayer doesn't depend on finding the right words. It rests on God, who wants to hear.

It's a child speaking to a father.
